title: Chatbots and the humanitarian sector
html:
In May 2018, a Facebook Messenger user could have interacted with over 300,000 unique chatbots. This past summer, Twitter estimated that 5% of its 139 million user base comprised of automated accounts.  Yet at the same time, the non-profit sector had very few examples of chatbot implementations. When Joanna Misiura joined me, she began exploring the idea of a humanitarian chatbot. The research eventually covered explaining the different “levels” of chatbots (think sophistication), what is already being done in the humanitarian sector, and topics that need to be considered before embarking on building a chatbot for use in our sector.  The final result - Chatbots in the humanitarian field - concepts, uses & shortfalls - aims to give anyone a quick introduction to chatbots, help them think through various issues/considerations, and hopefully enable them to make a quicker decision to proceed (or not).

Chatbots are not new. The first recognized chatbot was ELIZA - built in the 1960s. Obviously technology and chatbots have come a long way since then. And, along with the improvements come interesting possibilities ranging from community engagement to monitoring and evaluation to education. Story telling (Yeshi from charity:water), collection of needs (NeedsList), local prices & buyers (Farm.ink), farming support (FarmChat), and HIV/AIDS support (Marlo from UNAIDS) are all examples of recent chatbot implementations within the non-profit sector.

Although one must consider things like user design, an organization’s actual needs, government involvement/regulations, and infrastructure, I personally consider data to be one of the most important factors to think about. Do you have the data required to ‘make your chatbot smart’? The more advanced you want your chatbot to be, the more data it needs access to (in order to learn and improve).

As well, data ownership will be an extremely important consideration. The concerns involve what kind of data is collected, from whom, by whom and for what purpose. Although data collection for humanitarian purposes is done with good intention, security breaches can harm the most vulnerable of individuals. Recent scandals from Facebook and Google have proven that even the most powerful companies are not immune to cyberattacks. Chatbots targeted at vulnerable populations will have access to sensitive information. It is important to understand who has full access to this data, how it is used, and how long it will be kept. 

[PDF]

Looking beyond the “hype cycle”, there are many interesting possibilities for humanitarian sector chatbots. But, we will need focus, consolidation of effort, and willingness to share. In the end, organizations need to consider if a conversational agent is the right tool to help achieve its goals. While building a conversational agent is easier each year, new advances in technology require organizations to take more items into consideration. And, organizations need to realize that a chatbot is still a machine and only one method for engagement. 

Andrej
teaser: Research with Joanna Misiura on levels of chatbots, existing non-profit examples and what to consider before building one.
seo_description: Chatbots and the humanitarian sector: the types of chatbots, nonprofit examples such as NeedsList and Marlo from UNAIDS, and design and engagement considerations.
